questions.q: How does UNION/UNION ALL syntax differ across T-SQL, Oracle, MySQL, and PostgreSQL?
options: Oracle uses a different keyword for UNION
PostgreSQL requires a different clause order
MySQL does not support UNION ALL
It doesn't — UNION and UNION ALL are written identically on all four, in every version
questions.explain: UNION and UNION ALL have no dialect quirks at all across these four platforms — they are completely consistent.

questions.q: Which single platform in this course uses MINUS instead of EXCEPT for 'rows in the first query not in the second'?
options: MySQL
PostgreSQL
Oracle
T-SQL
questions.explain: T-SQL, PostgreSQL, and MySQL (8.0.31+) all use the ANSI-standard name EXCEPT; Oracle alone uses MINUS for the identical operation.

questions.q: What happens if you write EXCEPT against Oracle?
options: It works identically to MINUS
It silently behaves like UNION ALL
It works, but only inside a stored procedure
A syntax error — Oracle has never adopted the EXCEPT keyword
questions.explain: Oracle never adopted EXCEPT as a keyword, even though it's the ANSI-standard name used by every other platform in this course; Oracle code must use MINUS.

questions.q: Which MySQL version introduced support for INTERSECT and EXCEPT?
options: MySQL 8.0.0
MySQL has never supported INTERSECT or EXCEPT
MySQL 5.7
MySQL 8.0.31
questions.explain: MySQL added INTERSECT and EXCEPT in version 8.0.31 — earlier MySQL 8.0 releases and all of 5.7 and before support only UNION and UNION ALL.

questions.q: On a MySQL version before 8.0.31, how would a developer simulate EXCEPT?
options: By using MINUS instead
By using UNION ALL with DISTINCT
With a JOIN or a NOT EXISTS subquery
There is no way to simulate it at all
questions.explain: Before MySQL 8.0.31, INTERSECT and EXCEPT aren't available, so the same logic has to be expressed with a JOIN or a NOT EXISTS subquery instead.
